subject: English Language and Literature
content: Telling stories. The aim is to allow students to learn about how and why stories of different kinds are told. Students explore how language choices help to shape representations of different worlds and perspectives, including narratives that construct different views of a particular place, prose fiction that constructs imaginary worlds, and poetry that constructs a strong sense of personal perspective.

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Methods of language analysis. Students learn about and apply methods of language analysis, focusing on: phonetics, phonology and prosodics (e.g., sounds of speech, rhyme, alliteration); lexis and semantics (e.g., connotations, metaphor, idiomatic language); grammar (e.g., use of pronouns to shape narrative viewpoints); pragmatics (e.g., assumptions about listeners/readers); discourse (e.g., features of text types, visual design, and layout).

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Remembered places. Students study the AQA Anthology: Paris, exploring speech and non-literary material. They examine how writers and speakers present places, societies, people, and events, considering: representation and viewpoint; the metaphorical nature of narrative; contextual factors (time period, race, class, gender); affordances and limitations of different media; generic conventions; and how people and relationships are realised through language choices. This section is closed book in the exam.

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Imagined worlds. Students study one prose fiction text from a prescribed list (e.g., Mary Shelley's 'Frankenstein') to explore point of view and genre in constructing imaginary worlds.

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Poetic voices. Students study one poetry text from a prescribed list to explore the forms and functions of poetic voice.

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Exploring conflict. This section focuses on how language choices construct ideas of conflict between people and between people and their societies, including: the role of the individual in society, re-creative writing, critical commentary, and conflict in drama.

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Methods of language analysis. Underpins Component 2, focusing on the same analytical methods as 3.1.1 but applied to conflict-related texts.

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Writing about society. Students engage in re-creative writing based on set texts, exploring the role of the individual in society.

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Critical commentary. Students evaluate their own re-creative writing, reflecting on language choices and their effects.

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Dramatic encounters. Students study one drama text from a prescribed list to explore conflict in dramatic works.

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Making connections. Students undertake a personal investigation exploring a specific technique or theme in both literary and non-literary discourse, integrating methods of language analysis.

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Methods of language analysis. Underpins Component 3, focusing on making connections between literary and non-literary texts using analytical methods.

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Aims of the assessment. The specification aims to develop students' ability to read critically, analyse, evaluate, and undertake independent research, preparing them for further study and employment.

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Assessment objectives. The assessment objectives include: demonstrating knowledge and understanding of texts and their contexts; analysing the ways language, form, and structure shape meanings; exploring connections across texts; evaluating texts critically; and producing clear, coherent, and accurate writing.

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Assessment weightings. Paper 1: 40% of A-level (100 marks); Paper 2: 40% of A-level (100 marks); Non-exam assessment: 20% of A-level (50 marks).

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Non-exam assessment marking criteria. The criteria for the personal investigation (2,500–3,000 words) include: depth of analysis, integration of literary and non-literary texts, use of language methods, coherence, and critical reflection.

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Students explore the imagined worlds of the following texts which are characterised by unusual narratives, narrators and events: Mary Shelley's 'Frankenstein' (1818), Bram Stoker's 'Dracula', Margaret Atwood's 'The Handmaid’s Tale', and Alice Sebold's 'The Lovely Bones'. Students consider key aspects of the texts which place them in particular contexts of production and reception. Students analyse the language choices made by writers to study: point of view, characterisation, presentation of time and space/place, and narrative structure. This section of paper 1 is open book, allowing students to take a copy of their set text(s) into the exam without annotations or additional notes.

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Students study poems from one of four poets within the AQA Poetic Voices Anthology: John Donne, Robert Browning, Carol Ann Duffy, and Seamus Heaney. The prescribed poems for each poet are specified. This part of the subject content focuses on the nature and function of poetic voice in the telling of events and the presentation of people. Students explore and analyse: the presentation of time (understanding the past, reviewing past experiences, manipulation of time), the importance of place (locations and memories, their capture in voice(s), and their effect on individuals), how people and relationships are realised through point of view, attitude, specific registers, physical descriptions, speech, and thought, and the presentation of events through the poet’s selection of material, narrative frames, and other poetic techniques. This section of paper 1 is open book.

subject: English Language and Literature
content: This part of the subject content focuses on how language choices help to construct ideas of conflict between people and between people and their societies. Students learn about the ways writers and speakers use language, focusing on broad questions such as: How do people interact? How do people claim power and position others in talk? How do people express identity? What communicative strategies do people use when in conflict with others? How do different groups or individuals make themselves heard? Students apply their knowledge to the study of texts about individuals in situations of conflict and: produce re-creative work to find an absent or underplayed perspective in the original text, write a critical reflection on the processes and outcomes involved in re-creative work, and study drama that explores conflicts at different levels from the domestic to the societal.

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Students learn about methods of language analysis, adopting a close language focus and identifying salient features of language used in texts. Areas of language analysis include: phonetics, phonology and prosodics (e.g., how aspects of spoken language are produced and interpreted), lexis and semantics (e.g., connotations of terms of address), grammar (e.g., how structural features express characters’ attitudes), pragmatics (e.g., assumptions made about listeners/readers), and discourse (e.g., conventions of drama texts).

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Students study one of four texts: Jon Krakauer's 'Into the Wild', Kate Summerscale's 'The Suspicions of Mr Whicher: or the Murder at Road Hill House', F. Scott Fitzgerald's 'The Great Gatsby', or Khaled Hosseini's 'The Kite Runner'. Students explore how writers: present people, their points of view, and their relationships with others; shape narrative structure and present events/time/places; reveal speech and thought processes of characters and narrators; and use situations of conflict to express ideas about societies and their values. Students develop skills to adapt and shape original material for re-creative tasks, including awareness of monologue and dialogue, changing point of view, genre, context, purpose, audience, or mode, and developing undeveloped aspects of narrative and characterisation.

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Students learn to write a critical commentary to evaluate their re-creative writing. They explain their own language choices and analyse their intentions in reshaping the writer’s original material, focusing on critical decisions made and the adaptation of the base text. The aim is to demonstrate conceptual understanding of choices and effects, as well as an understanding of the original text, including why original writers made specific choices.

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Students study one of four dramatic texts: William Shakespeare's 'Othello', Arthur Miller's 'All My Sons', Tennessee Williams's 'A Streetcar Named Desire', or Rory Kinnear's 'The Herd'. Students explore how conflicts are presented, the meanings inferred from language use, and the contextual reasons for these conflicts. They analyse how playwrights: represent natural speech features, use language to create distinctively different characters, show characters asserting power and positioning others, and use conflict to create dynamic narratives and address wider themes of the play. This section of paper 2 is open book.

subject: English Language and Literature
content: This part of the subject content focuses on language use in different types of text, requiring students to make active connections between a literary text and non-literary material based on a chosen theme or linguistic strategies. Students demonstrate their ability to initiate and sustain independent enquiry. Texts prescribed for study in examined units may not be chosen, but further texts by the same authors or from similar sources are acceptable. The non-literary material must form a good source of data for investigations.

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Students learn methods of language analysis, adopting a close language focus and identifying salient features of language used in texts. Areas of analysis include: phonetics, phonology and prosodics, lexis and semantics, grammar (including morphology), pragmatics, and discourse. The application of these areas depends on the specific topic chosen.

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Students produce an investigation of 2,500-3,000 words, structured into sections: Introduction and aim(s) (750 words), Review (300-500 words), Analysis (1,250 words), Conclusions (200-500 words), Appendix (extracts/data), and References. Examples of possible explorations include: comparison of openings in a novel and an autobiography, exploration of real and fictional events, representations of themes in literary and non-literary sources, and exploration of speech features in literature and real-world communication.

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Assessment objectives (AOs) for A-level English Language and Literature include: AO1 (Apply concepts and methods from integrated linguistic and literary study), AO2 (Analyse ways in which meanings are shaped in texts), AO3 (Demonstrate understanding of the significance and influence of contexts), AO4 (Explore connections across texts), and AO5 (Demonstrate expertise and creativity in the use of English). The overall weighting of these objectives is distributed across Paper 1, Paper 2, and Non-exam assessment.

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Demonstrate understanding of the significance and influence of the contexts in which texts are produced and received.

subject: English Language and Literature
content: Explore connections across texts, informed by linguistic and literary concepts and methods.
